summary: Reports the experience of one MIT group that implemented both the user and server sides of the new Telnet protocol. It discusses the Go-Ahead mechanism and gives suggestions for a smoother changeover, since the new Telnet is not compatible with the old one.

plainLanguage.summary: A team built the new version of the remote-login tool and wrote down tips for others, because the new version does not talk to the old one.

questions: what is go ahead in telnet
subtitle: Implementation experience with the new Telnet protocol

tldr.problem: The new Telnet protocol introduced incompatible changes from the old one, and the Go-Ahead mechanism (for full-duplex communication) is difficult to implement reliably across different operating systems.
tldr.mechanism: MIT implemented both server and client for the new Telnet, supporting options like Echo and Suppress Go-Ahead, and created an experimental socket to test the new protocol while keeping the old one running on the default socket.
tldr.outcome: The RFC proposes making Suppress Go-Ahead the default to improve compatibility, since only a few hosts actually need Go-Ahead and most systems struggle to detect when processes are waiting for input.

today: RFC 559 is a historical implementation report on the new Telnet protocol. It documents early deployment experience and proposals that influenced later Telnet specifications.

sections.title: New Telnet and Compatibility Problems
sections.content:
RFC 559 documents MIT's experience implementing the new Telnet protocol on both client and server sides. The new Telnet is not backward compatible with the old one, creating a deployment challenge. The RFC discusses implementation of key options: the ECHO option (for choosing between local and remote echoing), the Suppress Go-Ahead option, and several Telnet control sequences including Interrupt Process (IP), Erase Character (EC), Abort Output (AO), Are You There (AYT), Break, and Synch.

A core technical problem is the Go-Ahead (GA) mechanism, which is meant to signal when a server has finished sending and the client may start typing. However, the server cannot reliably detect when a user process is actually waiting for input, making reliable GA transmission difficult across different operating systems like ITS, TENEX, and DEC-10.
sections.plainLanguage: The new Telnet has many options and special signals. The hardest part is the "Go-Ahead" signal that tells your computer it is your turn to type. Servers do not really know when the user is ready, so it often gets it wrong.

sections.title: Implementation Strategies
sections.content:
MIT's server uses a 2.5-second idle timeout: if no output has been sent for that duration, the server sends a Go-Ahead and enters an I/O wait state. This works most of the time but is not guaranteed and may send extra Go-Ahead signals. The user-side implementation lets users change echo mode and handles special character functions (EC, EL, AO, AYT, BRK, SYNCH) by assigning them to easily-typed keys with defaults like backslash for escape.

To handle the old and new Telnet protocols simultaneously, MIT brought up an experimental server on socket 60 (octal 105) that runs full new-protocol behavior, while the default socket 1 runs in a compatibility mode that does not initiate option negotiation and does not send Go-Ahead unless specifically negotiated.
sections.plainLanguage: The server waits a couple of seconds and then guesses it is time to say "your turn." The client lets you customize which key means what. They ran the new system on a test socket and kept the old one running normally.

sections.title: Proposal for Suppress Go-Ahead as Default
sections.content: The RFC strongly recommends making Suppress Go-Ahead the default behavior. Most hosts do not actually need or use Go-Ahead signals; only AMES-67 and UCLA-CON require them. Making suppression the default would reduce unnecessary negotiation in the vast majority of cases and improve compatibility with both old and new Telnet clients. The protocol specification can still require all implementations to support a "send Go-Ahead option," ensuring sites that need it can request it, while others avoid the overhead and unreliability of guessing when to send signals.
sections.plainLanguage: Only two computers really care about the "your turn" signal. If you make the default "do not send it" instead of "send it," most things work better and the two that need it can still ask for it.
